abstract: We consider the fair allocation of indivisible goods with binary valuations. In this setting, the maximum Nash welfare rule, the leximin rule, and all additive welfarist rules with a strictly concave function coincide. We show that for any number of agents, this rule is the only rule that satisfies envy-freeness up to one good, strategyproofness, neutrality, minimal completeness, and invariance under disapproving unassigned goods (IDU). Moreover, we present an alternative characterization for two agents, where we replace IDU with non-redundancy and resource-monotonicity. In both characterizations, all axioms are necessary.
title: Fair division with binary valuations: Characterizations

abstract: China, the EU, and the US are all expanding their export controls on items with both civilian and military applications. This column combines data on US exports with a quantitative trade model to examine the effects of export controls on dual-use goods. When the US and its allies impose controls together, target countries’ imports of controlled goods fall 5.7 times as much as under unilateral US controls. Coordination delivers a larger security gain for the US, measured as the rise in US real military spending relative to target countries, at a similar cost to civilians in terms of incomes and prices of goods.
authors: Jingting Fan, Kyle Handley, Nuno Limão

abstract: Rising housing costs have intensified affordability crises across Europe. This column examines the drivers of this growth, its distributional effects on households, and implications for labour mobility. While the pre-global financial crisis rise in house prices was largely driven by credit supply, housing supply constraints have become a more important driver of prices in recent years. Housing affordability pressures are highly uneven across location, housing tenure, income groups, and the level of urbanisation, and have widened income and wealth gaps between owners and renters. Beyond distributional concerns, declining affordability also has adverse consequences for labour allocation and efficiency.
authors: Robert Beyer, Nina Biljanovska, Alexandra Fotiou, Morgan Maneely, Frederik Toscani

abstract: Improving the effectiveness of residential energy-saving interventions is an important policy issue in demand-side management, yet such interventions are often constrained by the attitude-behavior gap and the difficulty of sustaining behavioral change over time. In addition, evidence remains limited on how intervention effects vary with household demographic and psychological heterogeneities. Drawing on a 16-week field experiment involving 267 households in Singapore, this study evaluates a combined intervention based on goal setting and information framing by integrating hourly electricity-use records with a structured questionnaire of 88 items covering energy-saving behaviors, personality traits, thinking styles, values, and demographic characteristics. Using a difference-in-differences framework with two-way fixed effects, this study estimates both the average and heterogeneous effects of the combined intervention. The results show that the largest average reduction in residential energy consumption across the combined interventions was 5.3%. From the perspective of heterogeneity, high-income and highly educated households are particularly responsive to environmental framing, with energy-saving effects reaching 5.39% and 5.62%, respectively. In the 10% monetary group, a one-unit increase in conscientiousness was associated with an estimated increase in electricity savings of approximately 11.6 percentage points. These findings underscore the importance of targeted demand-side policies rather than uniform intervention strategies. Specifically, with the energy-saving goal held constant, environmental framing yielded larger estimated electricity savings than monetary framing among high-income and highly educated households. Conscientiousness, altruistic values, and a holistic locus of attention were associated with greater energy savings under monetary framing. Overall, this study provides policy-relevant evidence for designing targeted and cost-effective residential energy conservation policies.
title: Targeting residential energy conservation through combined goal setting and information framing: Evidence from a field experiment in Singapore

abstract: The number of Nash equilibria of the mixed extension of a generic finite game in normal form is finite and odd. This raises the question how large the number can be, depending on the number of players and the numbers of their pure strategies. Here we present a lower bound for the maximal possible number in the case of n -player games where each player has two pure strategies. It is surprisingly close to a known upper bound.
title: Maximal number of mixed Nash equilibria in generic games where each player has two pure strategies

abstract: We study a dynamic political economy model in which two ideologically opposed parties alternate in power and set a one-dimensional policy that becomes the next period’s status quo. Policy change is costly, with costs potentially distributed asymmetrically between the parties. Pareto-efficient policy paths are monotone, and constant policies are efficient if and only if moderate. We characterize stationary Markov perfect equilibria in cutoff strategies: parties correct extreme status quos and maintain moderate ones. Policy reversals arise only under high polarization, when the equilibrium is unique and features perpetual reversals. High adjustment costs do not ensure efficiency: an incumbent cost advantage induces preemptive overshooting, whereas an opposition advantage produces free-riding and inaction. When polarization and cost imbalance are both low, all steady-state equilibrium policies are efficient. With convex rather than linear adjustment costs, inertia takes the form of gradualism. From an extreme status quo under high or very low polarization, welfare is locally highest when costs are balanced; from a moderate status quo, higher costs can improve welfare by dampening policy fluctuations.
title: Efficiency with Political Power Dynamics and Costly Policy Change

abstract: Religious rituals often generate synchronized economic activity and large-scale movement of people and goods with important public health consequences. This paper studies the link between the Islamic festival of Eid al-Adha, which mandates ritual animal sacrifice, and livestock infections. Using a new country–product–month panel comprising sixty Muslim countries and three halal livestock categories from 2004 to 2019, we examine whether Eid related international trade exposure or domestic livestock circulation result in higher livestock infections. Results show that country–product pairs with greater historical exposure to live animal imports during Eid periods experience significantly larger increases in livestock infections around Eid. Health impacts dissipate rapidly, vanishing after two months. In contrast, estimates based on domestic mobility exposure are sensitive to alternative functional forms, regional composition, and road infrastructure measures, precluding robust inference about this channel. The findings document a previously underexplored channel through which large-scale religious rituals may influence animal health and disease transmission.
title: Religious rituals, livestock mobility and infectious diseases: Evidence from Eid al-Adha

abstract: Since mid-1980s. convergence literature has proposed or examined empirically the following hypothesis: a) poorer countries’ incomes grow faster, b) their income level grows more than the income level of richer countries, c) resulting in convergence in income levels across countries. This paper emphasizes that faster growth in incomes, or β-convergence, does not imply a reduction in income differences. We define the convergence rate and directly test the convergence hypothesis. With data from three different sources (World Development Indicators, Maddison Project database, and Penn World Tables) from 1960 to 2024, we demonstrate unconditional and conditional divergence from the smallest (OECD) to the largest group of countries. Further, both in general and for the OECD, the lower the initial income greater is the divergence rate and this pattern is stronger for higher income countries. We show it is the divergence of TFP from the world technological frontier that explains divergence in incomes.
title: Divergence: Unconditional, Conditional and in OECD
